However, molten salt TES is a poor technology fit for integration with parabolic trough and linear Fresnel technologies that deliver heat at 310 oC due to its high cost, high freezing point limiting its temperature cycling range, and parasitic heating energy losses to avoid solidification in pipes and tanks. Large molten salt TES systems have also suffered from reliability challenges in the Crescent Dunes and Noor Ouarzazate III projects causing significant economic loss [6,7]. The leaks have mostly occurred in the floors of hot-salt tanks associated with improper design and fabrication procedures leading to high residual stress after welding fabrication, high stress during operation, stress relaxation cracking (SRC), buckling, and creep [6]. A potentially competing technology in the temperature range of interest is two-tank oil storage concept. However, the high cost of thermal oil ($2500 to $5000 per ton) makes the storage cost prohibitively expensive in that case, too [8] and could potentially suffer from similar failure issues as the two-tank molten salt TES. Other sensible-based solid- state thermal storage media (concrete, rocks) are being investigated (e.g., EnergyNest, Brenmiller, Siemens Gamesa, Polar Night Energy), but suffer from inherent challenges related to high cost, poor thermal responsiveness, thermal cyclic stability concerns, and Page 6 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. large footprint. The main challenge associated with concrete based TES systems is heat transfer. Heat transfer is problematic due to the conduction dominated thermal transport from HTF to concrete, which has poor thermal conductivity. The limitations of direct (no pipes) rock-based TES systems are low thermal conductivity, oil degradation in contact with solid media, thermal ratcheting due to difference in thermal expansion of the tank wall and solid filler material causing undesirable mechanical stress and potential tank failure, and high pumping costs associated with the high pressure drop through porous bed of rocks resulting in lower round-trip efficiency. Element 16 is developing sulfur TES to solve the two main challenges preventing state-of-the-art molten salt’s use for low-to-medium temperature industrial process heat. First is cost. Most of the cost of the molten salt heat storage system is the salt itself, which is generally about $1,200 per ton. Sulfur is about $60 per ton, changing TES economics on an order-of-magnitude scale. Second is operation temperature range. Since molten nitrate salts solidify around 220-240 °C, they primarily operate only above 265°C with extensive electrical heat tracing of tanks, equipment and pipes to prevent solidification (or risk breaking the heat storage, heat exchanger equipment, pumps, piping and valves). The operational expenses associated with electrical heat tracing can result in high levelized cost of storage. Element 16’s sulfur TES employs a single-tank design with heat transfer fluid (HTF) tubes located within molten sulfur stored in a pressure vessel (Figure 1). This configuration provides improved reliability by avoiding sulfur pumping, enabling sulfur to safely solidify, such as during maintenance, without damaging storage or heat transfer equipment.
